engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Pin
chess.body: A pin prevents a piece from moving because moving it would expose a more valuable piece behind it. Absolute pin = pinned to the king (piece cannot move legally). Relative pin = pinned to queen/rook (can move but it's a blunder). Identify pins in every position. Then exploit them.

wisdom.title: The Identity Question
wisdom.body: Who are you when the job title is gone, when the market is closed, when your daughter is asleep? Define yourself by what you do, not what you've achieved. 'I am someone who learns daily. I love deeply. I show up.' These don't depend on AED 30K or a Dubai visa. They're yours now.

book.author: James Clear
book.chapter: Identity-Based Habits: Become the Person First
book.lesson: Most people start with outcomes (lose 10kg), then think about processes (exercise), and never examine identity (I am someone who moves their body daily). Clear argues you should flip it. Start with identity: who do you want to become? Every action you take is a vote for that identity. Cast enough votes and the identity solidifies. A smoker trying to quit says 'I'm trying to quit.' A non-smoker says 'I don't smoke.' Same external action, completely different internal frame — and the internal frame determines long-term behaviour.
book.key_quote: The most practical way to change who you are is to change what you do.
book.action: Pick one identity statement: 'I am a daily learner.' 'I am someone who finishes what they start.' Then find one action today that votes for that identity.
crux: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
1% better daily compounds to 37x in a year. 1% worse decays to 0.03x.
Habits form on a four-step loop: cue → craving → response → reward.
Build good habits: make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Invert all four to break one.
Identity drives behaviour, not the reverse. 'I don't smoke' beats 'I'm trying to quit'.
Every action is a vote for the person you are becoming. Majority wins, not unanimity.
The two-minute rule: a new habit must take under two minutes to start.
Environment beats willpower. Motivation is overrated; friction is decisive.
Habit stacking: after [existing habit], I will [new habit]. The old habit becomes the cue.
You need a plateau of latent potential. Results lag effort — most people quit inside the lag.
Never miss twice. One miss is an accident. Two is the start of a new habit.
Measure what you want to repeat. An unrecorded habit drifts within three weeks.
learnings: Discipline is a design problem, not a character problem.
The gap between effort and visible result is where nearly everyone quits.
Systems survive bad days. Motivation does not.
Tracking is not admin. Tracking is the habit.
examples: British Cycling went from one Tour de France win in 110 years to five in six years by stacking 1% gains — pillow hygiene, hand-washing, bike paint for dust visibility.
Clear's own recovery: a bat to the face at 15, two years of rebuilding, then an academic All-American — built entirely on sleep and study routines, not talent.
Twice-weekly gym attendance beats a 90-minute session once a month, even though the monthly total is similar. Frequency builds identity; volume does not.
adapt: Score one caption per day before posting. The score is the habit, not the post.
Two-minute rule on the Dubai job hunt: open the tracker and add one company. That is the whole commitment.
SIP on auto-debit the day salary lands. Remove the monthly decision entirely.
Never miss twice on the daily brief. One skipped morning is fine. Two means the system broke.

minimalism.title: The Cost Of A Bigger House
minimalism.body: More space does not reduce clutter; it raises the threshold at which clutter becomes visible. People fill whatever they have. Then they pay to heat, clean, and furnish it.
minimalism.action: Before upgrading space, try emptying the space you have.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Reply Within 24 Hours, Even If Only To Acknowledge
etiquette.body: A three-word acknowledgement beats a perfect reply a week late. Silence is read as disregard, never as busyness. 'Got this — proper answer Thursday' costs eight seconds.
etiquette.action: Clear every message older than 24 hours with an acknowledgement.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: High Thinking Requires Simple Living
stillness.body: The phrase is one instruction, not two. Complexity of life consumes exactly the capacity that deep thought requires. Cut the first to afford the second.
stillness.action: Name the most complicated part of your week. Remove one layer.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Hanlon's Razor
model.body: Never attribute to malice what incompetence, tiredness, or a missed email explains. The uncharitable read is usually wrong and always expensive.
model.action: Reinterpret one recent slight as a mistake rather than an intent.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: Closing a first meeting warmly without committing to a date.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: The 3-Statement Link
drill.body: Net income flows to retained earnings and to the top of cash flow. Closing cash lands on the balance sheet. If you cannot recite this cold, every model you build is fragile.
drill.action: Draw all three statements and every link from memory. No reference.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Train Balance Before You Need It
health.body: Falls are a leading cause of injury death in older adults, and balance declines silently from midlife. It is trainable at any age and takes 60 seconds a day.
health.action: Stand on one leg, 30 seconds each side. Eyes closed to progress.
health.label: Health

quote.name: John D. Rockefeller
quote.quote: Don't be afraid to give up the good to go for the great.

lesson.lesson: Character is how you treat those who can do nothing for you.

case.title: OYO: Growth Before Foundation
case.story: OYO expanded to 80+ countries in 5 years. No standardized product, operational chaos, $600M losses. Had to shut down hundreds of hotels and lay off 5,000 people.
case.lesson: Blitzscaling works only if the unit economics work. Expand when you've proven the model, not before. Speed without structure is just expensive chaos.

fpna.title: SaaS Metrics
fpna.body: ARR, MRR, Churn, NRR, CAC, LTV. In tech FP&A, know these cold.

cfo.title: FC Step 2: IFRS Mastery
cfo.body: IFRS 16 (leases), IFRS 9 (financial instruments), IFRS 15 (revenue recognition) — these are the FC's bread and butter in Dubai/GCC. Know them technically AND practically. Interviewers will test this. Study one standard per week.

money_hack.title: No Lifestyle Inflation
money_hack.body: Got a raise? Don't upgrade lifestyle. Invest the increment for 3 years.

dubai.title: Notice period is a negotiation, not a fact
dubai.body: Gulf employers plan around a 30-day joiner. A 90-day Indian notice period kills live mandates. Buy-out clauses exist in most Indian contracts and employers routinely fund them.
dubai.targets: Say the real number early. Discovering it in week six loses the offer.
dubai.action: Find out your buy-out amount now. It is a line in the contract.

desk.productivity: Clear inbox to zero before 9 AM. Empty inbox = no mental overhead.

father.title: Vary who holds her
father.do: Hand her to grandparents, friends, and colleagues while you stay visible in the room.
father.why: Stranger wariness peaks around now. Practising handovers while you remain in sight teaches that unfamiliar people are safe, without forcing separation at the same time.

father.title: Sit her up and step back
father.do: Sit her unsupported on a soft surface within arm's reach, and let her balance.
father.why: Independent sitting typically consolidates around 7–8 months. Constant propping delays the postural adjustments she needs to make herself.

life_wisdom.teaching: The vow limits accumulation. Applied beyond property, hoarding commitments is a form of grasping — saying yes to everything is acquisitiveness in a respectable costume.
life_wisdom.apply: Say no to one thing this week that you would normally accept out of reflex rather than interest.

life_wisdom.translation: Work that does not require harm
life_wisdom.teaching: One of the eightfold path's least discussed elements: how you earn matters as much as how you behave outside earning.
life_wisdom.apply: Ask whether any part of your work depends on someone else not understanding something. That is the test, and it applies to finance more than most fields.

spanish.word: no tener pelos en la lengua
spanish.es: Ella no tiene pelos en la lengua.
spanish.en: She does not mince her words.

vocab.note: Signals scepticism without accusation. Powerful in a review meeting.

vocab.example: Give the country teams latitude on promotions, not on pricing.
vocab.note: A leadership word — defines the boundary rather than the rule.

speaking.title: Cut the throat-clear
speaking.drill: Notice and eliminate the meaningless opener: 'So…', 'Yeah, so…', 'I guess…'.
speaking.why: It signals you started talking before you started thinking, even when you did not.

interview_tech.q: How does IFRS 16 change the picture for a retailer with 60 leases?
interview_tech.a: Operating leases come on balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Rent expense is replaced by depreciation plus interest, so EBITDA rises — often materially for retail — while EBIT moves little. Interest is front-loaded, so early-life leases depress net income versus the old treatment. Watch three consequences: gearing ratios jump and can breach covenants written pre-IFRS 16; EBITDA-based multiples are no longer comparable to history; and store-level return metrics need restating or you will misjudge performance.

interview_tech.q: Explain working capital optimisation to a non-finance retail board.
interview_tech.a: Working capital is cash tied up in running the business — stock on shelves and money owed to you, less money you owe suppliers. Every day of stock is cash sitting in a warehouse instead of in the bank. Frame it in days and rupees, not ratios: 'we hold 95 days of stock; every day we cut releases AED 1.1M in cash we can spend on new stores instead of borrowing.' Boards act on that. They do not act on 'DIO improved 4%.'

interview_soft.q: What do you know about our company?
interview_soft.a: The disqualifying answer is anything from the homepage. Come with: their last reported results and one number from them, their format or brand mix and how it differs from peers, one strategic move in the last 18 months, and one question you genuinely cannot answer from outside. For a Gulf retail group that means knowing their franchise portfolio, which markets they operate directly versus through partners, and their exposure to mall footfall.

interview_soft.q: How do you build credibility in the first 90 days in a new company?
interview_soft.a: Deliver one visible thing early and be accurate about everything. Concretely: get the close done cleanly, learn the actual business by walking the stores rather than reading the reports, and find the one number everyone argues about and fix its definition. Do not restructure anything in the first quarter. Credibility in finance is cumulative and fragile — it comes from being right repeatedly, not from an early bold move.
